prior_approach.content: Borophene was prepared using a previously described growth-from-below method on metallic substrates.
prior_approach.evidence_span: borophene was prepared by a “growth from below” approach, as described elsewhere for a variety of metallic substrates30,36,37.

prior_approach.content: It is known from prior work that borophene rapidly oxidizes in oxygen or ambient conditions.
prior_approach.evidence_span: In contrast, borophene oxidizes rapidly under exposure to oxygen or ambient conditions30.

inspiration_source.content: The stacking-sequence test relies on the known chemical inertness of hBN used as a protective capping layer.
inspiration_source.evidence_span: To verify our hypothesis regarding the stacking sequence, we made use of the well-established chemical inertness of hBN. Therefore, hBN is commonly used as a protective capping layer for sensitive two-dimensional materials and nanostructures against oxidation50,51.

causal_claim.content: Registry variation between hBN and Ir causes undulation that produces moiré satellite spots.
causal_claim.evidence_span: The periodic change of registry between the hBN and the underlying substrate causes an undulation of the 2DM, in turn producing the satellite spots of the moiré pattern35.

causal_claim.content: High temperature and low precursor pressure cause borazine dissociation; nitrogen desorbs and boron dissolves into Ir near-surface region.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Using a significantly higher temperature, Tg = 1140 ◦C, and lower precursor pressure, pdose = 1×10−7 mbar, the borazine dissociates into its elemental constituents; nitrogen desorbs, while boron dissolves into the near-surface region of the Ir substrate.

causal_claim.content: Cooling below about 890 °C reduces boron solubility and induces segregation and borophene formation.
causal_claim.evidence_span: During subsequent cooling below ∼890 ◦C, the reduced boron solubility induces segregation to the surface and thereby the formation of borophene.

causal_claim.content: Coexisting rotational domains on the threefold substrate make the diffraction pattern appear hexagonal via incoherent superposition.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Because three rotational domains coexist on the threefold-symmetric substrate, their incoherent superposition produces an apparently hexagonal diffraction pattern.

causal_claim.content: Weaker Ir diffraction spots indicate formation of a two-layer vertical heterostructure on Ir.
causal_claim.evidence_span: This weakened Ir spot intensity indicates the formation of the two-layer vertical heterostructure on top of the Ir surface.

causal_claim.content: Stronger borophene-Ir binding explains the absence of the bell-shaped diffuse component in borophene.
causal_claim.evidence_span: In contrast, it is absent in the bottom profile, consistent with the much stronger binding of borophene to the Ir substrate39,44.

causal_claim.content: Reciprocal-space convolution shows electrons are diffracted coherently by both hBN and borophene.
causal_claim.evidence_span: This convolution in reciprocal space is equivalent to a multiplication of the real space scattering amplitudes of the two layers, and thus shows that the incident electrons are diffracted coherently by both the hBN and the borophene layer.

causal_claim.content: Reducing the initial boron loading duration led to only partial borophene coverage, allowing simultaneous imaging of hBN and heterostructure.
causal_claim.evidence_span: the duration of the initial boron loading of the Ir substrate was reduced. This lead to a partial coverage with borophene and enabled to simultaneously image both, the hBN reference phase and the heterostructure

causal_claim.content: The weak extra height modulation in the heterostructure is attributed to vertical stacking with hBN.
causal_claim.evidence_span: The weak superimposed height modulation is not observed for bare borophene and is therefore attributed to the vertical stacking with the hBN layer30.

causal_claim.content: Weak hBN-related STM features and reduced apparent height reflect modified electronic properties of hBN in the heterostructure.
causal_claim.evidence_span: The weak, hBN-related features within the heterostructure region, together with the reduced apparent height of this phase [see Fig. 2(b)], reflect the modified electronic properties of the hBN layer in the heterostructure.

causal_claim.content: Weak interaction permits rotational disorder of hBN domains, causing moiré spot broadening in LEED.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Consequently, the weak interaction allows for rotational disorder of the hBN domains, which causes the broadening of moiré spots, as observed in the LEED measurements shown in Fig. 1(c).

causal_claim.content: The top hBN layer protects underlying borophene from oxidation.
causal_claim.evidence_span: This result demonstrates that the top hBN layer effectively protects the underlying borophene against oxidation.

causal_claim.content: Increasing borazine pressure and lowering temperature shifts the chemistry toward hBN layer formation.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Upon increasing the dosing pressure by one order of magnitude to pdose = 1×10−6 mbar and lowering the growth temperature to Tg = 960 ◦C, the chemical balance shifts toward formation of an hBN layer33.

causal_claim.content: Cooling to about 890 °C causes dissolved boron to segregate back to the surface and form borophene beneath hBN.
causal_claim.evidence_span: During subsequent cooling to approximately 890 ◦C, dissolved boron segregates back to the surface as described by Omambac et al.30. In the present case, it forms a borophene layer underneath the hBN overlayer.

causal_claim.content: If boron atoms are deeper than their diffusion length, segregation is suppressed and a boron-depleted near-surface region forms.
causal_claim.evidence_span: If boron atoms are dissolved deeper in the bulk than their diffusion length, their segregation is suppressed, resulting in the formation of a boron-depleted region directly beneath the surface30,56.

causal_claim.content: Ambient-stability findings show hBN protects borophene from oxidation and confirm the Ir/borophene/hBN stacking sequence.
causal_claim.evidence_span: This finding shows that the hBN overlayer effectively protects borophene against oxidation, thereby confirming the stacking sequence Ir(111)/borophene/hBN.

mechanism_principle.content: The diffuse bell-shaped feature is associated with many weakly bonded 2D material systems.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: This pronounced feature is found for many weakly bonded two-dimensional material systems40–43.

mechanism_principle.content: The extra spots are explained by convolution of the borophene and hBN moiré reciprocal lattices.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: Their positions at 0.70 Å−1 and 1.98 Å−1 are naturally explained by a convolution of the two reciprocal lattices

mechanism_principle.content: Weaker moiré spots are explained by weaker hBN-borophene interaction as reported previously.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: The weaker moiré spots of the heterostructure can be explained by a weaker interaction between hBN and borophene, as reported by Cuxart et al.19.

mechanism_principle.content: hBN contributes weakly to tunneling because its insulating character makes it mostly transparent in STM.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: The hBN contributes only weakly to the tunneling current, consistent with its insulating character which makes hBN mostly transparent to the STM49.

hypothesis_statement.content: The authors propose vertical stacking and coherent diffraction in the heterostructure.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: To further support the hypothesis of vertical stacking and coherent diffraction

hypothesis_statement.content: These STM observations suggest hBN is electronically decoupled by borophene and forms the top layer of the vertical heterostructure.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: This observation suggests that the hBN layer is electronically decoupled from the Ir substrate by the borophene layer and therefore forms the top layer of this vertical heterostructure.

evidence_result.content: The heterostructure LEED pattern contains more diffraction features than either reference structure.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The LEED pattern of the heterostructure, shown in Fig. 1(c), exhibits a significantly richer set of diffraction features than the two reference structures.

evidence_result.content: hBN and heterostructure profiles show broad bell-shaped diffuse intensity under integer-order spots, unlike borophene.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Both, the hBN and heterostructure line profiles exhibit the so-called bell-shaped component, i.e., very broad diffuse intensity with a FWHM on the order of 50 % of the Brillouin zone, underlying all integer-order diffraction spots.

evidence_result.content: Additional heterostructure diffraction spots cannot be explained by a simple incoherent sum of hBN and borophene patterns.
evidence_result.evidence_span: However, additional spots appear that cannot be accounted for by a simple incoherent superposition of the two patterns.

evidence_result.content: The convolution-based diffraction model reproduces the experimentally observed heterostructure spot manifold.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The resulting model pattern reproduces the manifold of diffraction spots observed experimentally in Fig. 1(c).

evidence_result.content: The model also reconstructs the two heterostructure-only spots.
evidence_result.evidence_span: In particular, the two spots only found in the heterostructure linescan can also be reconstructed by the model

evidence_result.content: The heterostructure STM region shows stripe-like corrugations with ~1.4 nm spacing matching borophene's (6×2) periodicity.
evidence_result.evidence_span: the measured spacing between adjacent stripes is ∼1.4 nm, corresponding to the lateral sixfold periodicity of the (6 × 2) reconstruction of borophene.

evidence_result.content: After air exposure, bare borophene's (6×2) diffraction disappears and diffuse intensity remains, indicating oxidation.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The characteristic (6 × 2) diffraction spots disappear completely. Instead, only weak and diffuse intensity remains in the region between the specular (00) spot and the first-order diffraction spots of the Ir substrate, clearly indicating oxidation of the borophene layer.

evidence_result.content: The authors conclude borophene lies between Ir and hBN, consistent with prior work.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Thus, we conclude that borophene is located between the Ir substrate and the hBN layer above. This interpretation is consistent with previous work from Auwärter and co-workers19.

evidence_result.content: No diffraction change during initial loading is consistent with precursor dissociation, desorption of N and H, and B dissolution into Ir bulk.
evidence_result.evidence_span: At this stage, no change in the diffraction pattern is observed, consistent with adsorption of the precursor and dissociation into its elemental constituents: nitrogen and hydrogen desorb as molecules53,54, whereas boron dissolves into the Ir bulk30.

evidence_result.content: Uniform LEEM contrast indicates the heterostructure covers the Ir surface with high lateral uniformity.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The homogeneous contrast in Fig. 4(c) indicates that the resulting Ir(111)/borophene/hBN heterostructure extends laterally with high spatial uniformity, covering the entire Ir substrate’s surface.

evidence_result.content: The change from single steps to step bunches provides additional evidence for borophene formation beneath hBN.
evidence_result.evidence_span: This pronounced restructuring of the Ir surface provides additional evidence for borophene formation beneath the hBN top layer, consistent with the step-bunching previously reported for borophene on Ir(111)30.

evidence_result.content: SPA-LEED confirms vertically stacked, structurally unaffected layers; STM indicates weak interaction of hBN with its support.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The structural characterization by SPA-LEED confirms the vertical stacking of the two structurally unaffected two-dimensional materials, while the STM study indicates the characteristic ease of interaction between hBN and its support.

evidence_result.content: Real-time LEEM shows homogeneous heterostructure formation across the entire surface.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Real-time LEEM further shows that the heterostructure forms homogeneously across the entire surface.

constraint.content: Temperature must stay above about 890 °C to prevent boron segregation from the subsurface region.
constraint.evidence_span: It is crucial to keep the temperature above ∼890 ◦C to prevent the segregation of the boron in the subsurface region30.

constraint.content: Heterostructure formation requires crossing the phase boundary between borophene and hBN growth by changing pressure or temperature.
constraint.evidence_span: the heterostructure formation can be achieved either by increasing pdose or by decreasing Tg, provided that the phase boundary, separating borophene formation from hBN growth in the phase diagram shown in Fig. 4(b) of Ref. 33, is crossed.

contradiction.content: Unlike bare borophene, the heterostructure diffraction pattern is essentially unchanged after air exposure.
contradiction.evidence_span: In striking contrast, the diffraction pattern of the heterostructure remains essentially unchanged after exposure to ambient conditions.

contradiction.content: In contrast to bare borophene, the heterostructure remains structurally unchanged after ambient exposure.
contradiction.evidence_span: In contrast to borophene, the heterostructure remains structurally unchanged upon exposure to ambient conditions.
